Thesis - AIRJ is a company trying to turn hot air and humidity into something useful. When machines run, like data centers or factories, they create heat, and a lot of that heat is normally wasted. AIRJ is trying to use that wasted heat to pull moisture out of the air.

When you pull moisture out of air, two useful things happen at once. You get water and you make the air easier and cheaper to cool.

1. Start with the water.

AIRJ is first and foremost a “water from air” company. The claim is that it can produce distilled water using low amounts of energy by using leftover heat, which it says is much more efficient than normal ways of pulling water from air. So in places where water is expensive or hard to access, the system could produce usable water and a data center could turn heat it was going to waste anyway into water it can actually use.

2. Then there is the cooling side.

This is really the same idea used in a different way. Removing humidity from air and cooling buildings normally takes a lot of electricity, and a big part of that is dealing with moisture in the air. AIRJ is trying to use heat instead of electricity for that step. Early tests show up to around 40% energy savings versus desiccant wheel systems in some setups, but results depend on conditions and it is not yet proven at large scale. If it holds up, the same system makes cooling cheaper.

It made no commercial revenue last quarter, and it does not expect meaningful revenue until 2027. The idea is that it could fit into large facilities like data centers, where cooling demand is rising fast because of AI. It has done pilot work with data center developers and has been involved in programs connected to companies like Microsoft, Google, Vertiv, Schneider Electric, and Danfoss. 

The idea is simple: if data centers need more cooling, more efficiency, and more water, AIRJ sits right in the middle of that problem.

Plus, AIRJ has a joint venture and commercialization relationship tied to GE Vernova, and it also has partnerships with BASF and Carrier for materials, manufacturing, and distribution. That gives it a real path to scale if the technology works.

But this is still early. It has to prove it works outside pilots, that it is cheaper than normal cooling systems and that big customers actually adopt it. Right now, customers want pilots before committing to larger deals and a lot of companies at this stage never make it past that step. It has about $35 million in cash with no debt which management says is enough to fund it through 2027.

If this works in real buildings at real scale, and data centers keep expanding the way they are, the company could matter a lot more than it does today and the upside is massive.

Not financial advice.
